WINNERS AND LOSERS
Winner: Cutter Gauthier scoring
The Ducks forward is having one of the greatest goal-scoring months in NHL history. He became the first player to record four hat tricks in a calendar month and the first player in more than 103 years to record four hat tricks in a span of nine games. He's scored 14 goals in 14 games, joining Gretzky as the only players age 22 or younger to do so. Gauthier now has 17 goals in November, putting him within reach of the NHL record for most goals in a month (20).

It's Cutter Gauthier's November; we're just living in it.

Loser: Cutter Gauthier conjecture
The better Gauthier does, the more revisionist history is dispensed around his decision not to play for the Flyers, the team that drafted him. The latest: GM Danny Briere refuting a report that his front office broke a promise to Gauthier about turning pro. He called it "nonsense" in a radio interview.

"This is just people trying to rehash things that happened in the past. We talked about it two years ago when it happened," Briere said. "It never came to my ears that there was any kind of promises."

Well, I'm sure that's the last we'll hear of this ...

Winner: Mortality
The Athletic's Dan Robson had a remarkable story about the mental health challenges of goaltenders this week. Calgary Flames netminder and amateur philosopher Devin Cooley was featured and revealed how he would sometimes process bad goals he'd given up: by scanning the crowd for "elderly people" and "thinking about how that person likely would die before him -- and therefore, no one would remember the bad goal he'd just given up." Goalies, man.

Loser: Fragility
What an absolute bummer it was to see Connor Bedard injured off a faceoff on Tuesday night. Grabbing his shoulder, tossing his stick, knowing the potential severity. He has 18 points in 15 games. It's horrendous we don't get to watch more of him.

Winner: Utah Mammoth

Utah's Winter Classic jersey is an instant classic, from the vivid blue to the faux throwback Mammoth.

Chris Armstrong, the team's president of hockey operations, told me it's a top-three Winter Classic jersey. He might not be wrong.

Loser: IIHF website
The International Ice Hockey Federation's website was hacked this week, as someone posted an image of Ilya Kovalchuk and the headline "Scared To Face Russia?" after the IIHF removed Russia from the upcoming world junior championship.

The IIHF website is now being rebuilt, with a temporary site currently up. Suggestion: Don't make the admin password "hockey" next time.

FAVORITE ON-ICE MOMENT

If goalie interference is the NHL's ultimate Rorschach test, goals scored on kicked pucks is right behind it for divergent perceptions. This one by the Devils' Connor Brown counted, with the NHL situation room ruling that "a puck that deflects into the net off an attacking Player's skate who does not use a 'distinct kicking motion' shall be ruled a goal."

I'm torn in this one. It's clearly a kick that propels the puck into the net and shouldn't have counted ... and yet it's an impressive bit of skill from Brown to knock that puck into the Capitals' net. It remains a little absurd that players are allowed to kick the puck to their stick or their teammate or out of the zone or anywhere that's not over the goal line.

So, in summary: This shouldn't have been a goal ... but I'm happy it was.

FAVORITE OFF-ICE MOMENT

At an Edmonton Save-On-Foods, giant depictions of Oilers stars Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl were created out of cases of soda. Put it in the Louvre.

MUST-SEE GAMES

Edmonton Oilers at Carolina Hurricanes

Sat., Nov. 21, 1 p.m. ET | ESPN+

The top two teams in the NHL entering Thursday night's games. Their last meeting in Edmonton on Oct. 22 was a bonkers 6-5 shootout win for the Oilers that saw Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl both post five-point games. This time, however, the Hurricanes will have Jordan Staal in the lineup.

Ottawa Senators at Florida Panthers

Wed., Nov. 25, 7 p.m. ET | ESPN+

Brady Tkachuk welcomes some old friends from Ottawa down to Sunrise after their contentious reunion up north last month.

San Jose Sharks at Anaheim Ducks

Wed., Nov. 25, 10 p.m. ET | ESPN+

Cutter Gauthier vs. Macklin Celebrini. NorCal vs. SoCal. Sharks vs. Ducks. There will be goals.

PUCK HEADLINES
Dateline: Pittsburgh
With the Penguins at 7-11-2 and playing wildly inconsistent hockey, Sidney Crosby's future is again becoming a topic of conversation around Pittsburgh.

GM Kyle Dubas met the media Wednesday and discussed the "unique circumstance" he faces with Crosby, Evgeni Malkin and Kris Letang. Two members of that trinity are unrestricted free agents after this season: Crosby and Malkin. Letang is signed through 2027-28.

Dubas said Crosby's situation is as unique as it gets.

"He's owed all the respect in the world," Dubas said. "If he wants to be here, that's great, and that's obviously what we would love as well."

But Dubas is a realist. If the Penguins don't turn things around, there will be trades of veterans for "future-oriented" returns. That shift in focus is as much a factor for the Penguins' three legends as their own advancing age.

"They're at an age where it's not just a given that they're always going to continue to play, either," Dubas said. "There's so many different variables, [like] our team performance, how they're feeling about things. I know we all wish them to play forever, but at some point the time comes."

Dateline: Detroit
A quick update on the ongoing Dylan Larkin and Simon Edvinsson drama:

1. The Detroit Free Press reported that the Red Wings are seeking "an established 30-goal scorer, preferably a center" in exchange for Larkin. Well ... it's good to want things, one supposes.

I can report that the Red Wings are open to other trade packages. One team that checked in on Larkin had Detroit asking for a young cornerstone center who could score 30 goals in the NHL but hadn't yet.

Ultimately, this remains a game of chicken. The Red Wings are waiting things out in the hopes that Larkin expands his trade list to teams that are willing to ante up in ways teams on his current 10-team list are not. Larkin is waiting in the hopes that Detroit eventually takes the best deal available, like Winnipeg did with the Devils' deal for Connor Hellebuyck -- and that the best deal is the one from the Minnesota Wild, his desired destination.

Who blinks? All we know is that Larkin's salary losses due to his suspension are due to cross $1 million this weekend.

2. Edvinsson has his own deadline. The restricted free agent must sign a contract by Dec. 1 at 5 p.m. ET, or he'll be ineligible to play in the NHL for the remainder of the 2026-27 season. The 23-year-old defenseman has been linked to the Boston Bruins, who have multiple first-round picks and a deep prospect pool. The San Jose Sharks have been circling Edvinsson, and Max Miller of Sharks Hockey Digest noted that Detroit assistant GM Kris Draper was scouting the Sharks recently.

One team that I believe is keeping an eye on Edvinsson is the Edmonton Oilers. It makes a ton of sense from an age perspective and the role he'd play. Edvinsson helped form one of the best defensive pairing in the league with Moritz Seider last season. Imagine him holding down the fort defensively next to Norris Trophy contender Evan Bouchard in Edmonton.

The clock keeps ticking ... who steps up to land Edvinsson?

stories.headline: Valentín Barco on Chelsea career so far: 'I think I can give a lot more'
stories.summary: Chelsea's Valentín Barco has said he is confident that he's still a long way away from reaching his full potential.
stories.body:
Chelsea's Valentín Barco has said he is confident that he's still a long way away from reaching his full potential.

The Argentina international returned to Chelsea this week having not featured in his country's two international friendlies, a 2-1 defeat to Uruguay and a 7-0 rout of Costa Rica.

"As a player, you always want to play so you are not happy when you don't but I understand this is the best national team in the world," Barco told ESPN. "But I'm happy to come to the national team, to continue to represent my country. I will now try to play at Chelsea and contribute."

Barco, 22, was part of Argentina's squad that finished runners-up to Spain at the 2026 World Cup.

He signed a contract with Chelsea through 2033 following his strong performances for Strasbourg, the club he joined from Brighton & Hove Albion in January 2025.

Returning to the Premier League was a priority for Barco, who made only seven appearances during his time at Brighton. Barco has had limited playing time under Xabi Alonso but said he believes he will eventually shine at Stamford Bridge.

"I think I can give a lot more," he said. "I also said the same thing when I was at Strasbourg; even when I was playing well, I knew I could give more because I know what I can give.

"I have a lot of confidence in myself so I have to keep working to continue growing."

Barco has one goal in even appearances, four of which in the Premier League.

stories.headline: Skubal to ...? What about other big free agents? How MLB offseason dominoes fall
stories.summary: Based on what ESPN's Jeff Passan is hearing, we predict where the top names available will land -- and how they impact each other.
stories.body:
The countdown to the impending lockout is getting closer, which means the MLB offseason will likely grind to a depressing halt when the clock hits midnight on Dec. 1. Until then, teams are continuing to act like it's business as usual -- Jake Bauers to the Boston Red Sox, Dustin May to the Chicago White Sox and Evan Phillips to the Atlanta Braves have been the most significant free agent signings so far.

The big prize in a weak class is two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal -- and he's expected to sign before the sport shuts down. This happened prior to the last lockout following the 2021 season, when Corey Seager, Marcus Semien, Javier Baez, Max Scherzer, Robbie Ray and Kevin Gausman all signed $100 million-plus contracts before the lockout went into effect.

Skubal might be the only nine-figure free agent this year, but the ripple effect of where he lands will dictate the offseason.

Using Jeff Passan's intel on what he's hearing will happen over the next two weeks as a guideline, let's kick off this offseason edition of dominoes with Skubal going ... East?

Tarik Skubal to New York Mets

The Mets are the favorite to land Skubal, according to Passan, in part because of the Los Angeles Dodgers' desire for a shorter-term commitment. Of course, Skubal loved his time with L.A. and lives in Arizona in the offseason, so maybe the Dodgers will view this as a situation of "sign him while you can" and eventually give Skubal whatever it takes.

If the labor negotiations do eventually end up with some sort of capped system, this could be the last chance for the Dodgers to empty their bank vault for several years. Their primary need for their long-term future -- regardless of payroll rules -- is getting younger in the lineup (Andy Pages was the only regular younger than 30 years old) rather than adding more starting pitching. Instead of locking up another starter, they might be eyeing the free agent class following the 2029 season for their next big signing: Elly De La Cruz, Brice Turang, Jordan Walker and, if they want to dip into pitching, Paul Skenes.

Enter the Mets, a big-market team with money to spend while the rules permit, holes in the rotation to fill and losing ways to mend. They have two young rotation anchors in Nolan McLean and Christian Scott, but some of their veteran additions haven't worked out, including last offseason's trade for Freddy Peralta or Sean Manaea's three-year deal two years ago. The Mets haven't had a pitcher finish in the top five of the Cy Young voting since Jacob deGrom in 2020; they need Skubal more than the Dodgers need him.

Michael King to San Diego Padres

The Padres' new owners appear willing to keep up the spending habits of the late Peter Seidler, so that's the good news. The bad news is they need to fill at least three-fifths of a rotation, with King, Walker Buehler, Robbie Ray, Casey Mize and Nick Pivetta all free agents (Randy Vasquez is the lone holdover and they're hoping for a comeback from Joe Musgrove, who returned in the postseason after missing two full seasons). Swiping Skubal from the Dodgers would be a double whammy -- helping yourselves while hurting your enemy -- but logic says the Padres need to spread the money around. Re-signing King, who has a 3.15 ERA in his three years in San Diego, should be the first step.

Trevor Rogers to Toronto Blue Jays

Are the Blue Jays interested in Skubal or are they interested in rotation help in general? Because after finishing last in the majors in runs scored, they definitely need to boost the lineup. Bottom line: After dropping to 79-83 in 2026, the Jays need to add an impact player or two no matter the position.

That might be Rogers, who ranks fifth among starting pitchers on ESPN's ranking of the top 50 free agents -- behind Skubal, Peralta, Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira and King -- but he might be the best combination of age (he's entering his age-29 season) and upside (3.16 ERA over the past two seasons).

Rogers isn't overpowering, but he possesses a five-pitch mix and induces a ton of chase while issuing just 39 walks in 30 starts for the Baltimore Orioles this past season. He does have some injury history -- missing most of 2023 with biceps and shoulder issues, and he had a knee injury at the start of 2025 -- but that also means he doesn't have a lot of wear on his left arm. The Blue Jays are dreaming of a Skubal/Dylan Cease combo, but Cease, Rogers, Jose Soriano and Trey Yesavage would rank as one of the top foursomes in the majors -- and there could still be room left to sign a hitter.

The one issue with Rogers is that he declined the qualifying offer the Orioles gave him, so the Blue Jays would lose their second- and fifth-highest draft picks as well as forfeit $1 million from their international pool money. Losing those picks will cool some teams on Rogers, but the Blue Jays, after coming so close in 2025, are determined to get back to the World Series.

Freddy Peralta to Baltimore Orioles

That leaves Peralta as the next pitcher in line. The Orioles "are everywhere," Passan reported, and have a willingness to carry a top-10 payroll -- which, according to Cot's Contracts, they last reached in 2005 (they were 14th in 2026). The Orioles were 17th in rotation ERA and face the prospect of losing Rogers, so they will be looking for a starter to join Shane Baz and Kyle Bradish to lead the rotation. This could be a best-case scenario: Rogers turned down the qualifying offer, so if he signs for more than $50 million with another team, the Orioles receive a draft pick at the end of the first round. Since Peralta was traded during his free agent season, he can be signed without any penalty.

Kaima Taira (and Clay Holmes) to Chicago Cubs

We know the Cubs need major help in terms of starting pitching -- they basically need to fill an entire rotation. Re-signing Holmes is a popular prediction, but they'll need more than him. The Cubs haven't signed a pitcher to a nine-figure deal since Yu Darvish in 2018, so that takes them out of the Skubal sweepstakes and perhaps Peralta as well, given his projected contract of four years, $96 million. They prefer not to sign free agents with qualifying offers, so that is likely to eliminate Rogers. The highest-ranked remaining starter would be the 5-foot-8 Taira, who had a 1.36 ERA in Japan in 2026.

Chicago went the Japan route three years and got three solid years from Shota Imanaga, but Taira has better stuff and shouldn't be as prone to the home run. His projected contract is five years for $72.5 million.

Randy Arozarena to Philadelphia Phillies

Let's move away from the pitching market to a big-market team looking to make a major signing. The Phillies need a hitter. Preferably right-handed. Preferably an outfielder. Preferably a good defender to help one of the more porous defenses in the majors. Perhaps someone who reportedly prefers to head back to the East Coast.

Passan reports that teams are balking at Arozarena's $100 million asking price, but with an aging roster that needs to win now, the Phillies might be the one team willing to get close to nine figures -- after all, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski isn't one to shy away from paying to get the guy he wants.

Arozarena had an outstanding under-the-radar season in Seattle in 2026, posting 5.7 WAR and leading the American League in runs scored despite playing in a tough hitters' park with a bad lineup around him. He's gone 20/20 all six of his full seasons in the majors and has been extremely durable, averaging 154 games over the past five seasons. He's a below-average defender in left field, but, hey, when do the Phillies care about defense anyway?

Seiya Suzuki to San Diego Padres

With Arozarena heading to the Phillies in our scenario, Suzuki is the next domino to fall ... going to San Diego. Besides their need for starting pitchers, the Padres have also been considering some of the bigger hitters, with Passan labeling the Padres the favorites to land Suzuki -- although, he also makes sense for the Seattle Mariners or returning to the Cubs.

Suzuki is coming off a .270/.368/.473 season with Chicago while posting the best defensive metrics of his career (88th percentile in outs above average and 94th percentile in arm value). A projected four-year, $90 million contract is steep for a player entering his age-32 season, but the Padres' window is closing the older Manny Machado and Xander Bogaerts get (with years to go on each of their contracts). The Padres would play Suzuki in right field and move Fernando Tatis Jr. back to the infield, probably second base, where he started 50 games last season.

Jazz Chisholm Jr. to Toronto Blue Jays

After signing Rogers, the Blue Jays still have work to do. Arozarena and Suzuki are possibilities, but Chisholm, with a two-year, $46 million projection, is a less expensive and younger option. While the Yankees seem content to let him walk after inconsistent results at the plate and lack of focus, Chisholm has averaged 2.9 WAR over each of the past three seasons and is an excellent defender at second base (at least via Statcast). He was worth 4.1 WAR in 2025, when he hit 31 home runs, but fell off to 1.7 in 2026. The Jays could turn Ernie Clement back into a super utility guy to play Chisholm at second base, plus Chisholm has the ability to shift into the outfield as needed.

Brandon Lowe to New York Yankees

With David Bednar accepting the Yankees' qualifying offer, general manager Brian Cashman can breathe a little easier about his bullpen and turn his attention to replacing Chisholm at second. Maybe Anthony Volpe is the guy. Or, after more than 2,000 plate appearances in the majors with an OPS+ of 83, maybe he's not. Lowe is a big upgrade in power -- he has hit 66 home runs over the past two seasons -- and played the best defense of his career after changing his pre-pitch routine. While it would be wonderful to see the Pittsburgh Pirates re-sign Lowe, his projected four-year, $80 million contract is more likely to place him in the Bronx than next to the Roberto Clemente Bridge.

Teruaki Sato to Los Angeles Angels

It will be fascinating to see what kind of deal the Japanese slugger lands. He looks a lot like Munetaka Murakami did a year ago, and Murakami had to settle for a lower-than-expected two-year, $34 million contract with the White Sox. He hit .207 for them this past season, but with 35 home runs and a ton of walks and strikeouts. The overall offensive package was productive, although Murakami hit .156 the final two months. It's hard to say how those results will affect the evaluations of Sato.

Sato was primarily a third baseman in Japan; if he can stay there, he could end up with the Phillies -- or the Yankees, except we have Lowe going to New York -- but most believe he'll end up in left field or first base. Maybe, like Murakami, Sato ends up in a surprise destination. The Angels were 28th in the majors in OPS at third base and need to take a risk to boost the offense. If Sato's defensive chops aren't up to par at third base, they can try him in left field.

Adrian Morejon to Los Angeles Dodgers

Where does this leave the Dodgers? There are other good starting pitchers out there: Tyler Mahle, Nick Martinez, Gausman, Imanaga, Foster Griffin. Given that May's deal with the White Sox is for three years and $52.5 million, much higher than expected, we'll see if the market now explodes for this group. The Braves, San Francisco Giants and Houston Astros are among the teams in the mix here, along with the Cubs and Padres. The Tampa Bay Rays will need to re-sign Martinez or replace him. Luis Arraez and Ian Happ are the other top position players.

None of those players feel like a fit for the Dodgers. Morejon, however, is one of the top relievers in the game. The Dodgers already lost Phillips, and Alex Vesia is also a free agent, so they could use a high-leverage reliever -- yes, even though Edwin Diaz and Tanner Scott are already two of the game's highest-paid relievers and signed for two more seasons.

Again, the rules might be changing. This could be one last chance for the Dodgers to play Moneyball.

stories.headline: Max Verstappen rejects F1's new biometric health plan for 'privacy' reasons
stories.summary: Max Verstappen has said he will not give permission to Formula 1 and its new partner Whoop to broadcast his biometric data during races.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen has said he will not give permission to Formula 1 and its new partner Whoop to broadcast his biometric data during races.

On Wednesday, F1 announced a new commercial partnership with fitness wearable company Whoop, including plans to incorporate biometric data from drivers in its future broadcasts.

Whoop devices have the potential to monitor the physiological metrics of the wearer, such as heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen level, skin temperature, sleep patterns, and stress.

According to an F1 press release, "a cornerstone of the partnership will be the development of new broadcast storytelling experiences, featuring select insights delivered in the right way in collaboration with the drivers to provide fans with a real-time window into the physical realities of racing."

Due to the personal nature of the data collected by a Whoop device, F1 would need permission from drivers to broadcast it.

Verstappen said he would not be willing to participate in the project and revealed he does not even monitor his own heart rate while training.

"I won't be involved," Verstappen was quoted as saying by Motorsport.com. "I don't use any device, also not for my training, I don't use anything. First of all, I don't like to be tracked and I know when I'm tired.

"If other drivers want to [share], then sure. But for me, it's not something that I like and also not something that I want people to see or that I want to show."

Asked if his decision was due to privacy, he added: "Yes, also that. People don't need to know my heart rate. I also don't want to know my heart rate! I know when it's high and I know when it's low.

"For me, it's definitely a privacy thing, but, as I said, I also don't use it privately for training either."

- Lando Norris, Max Verstappen confident in F1's decision to race in Middle East

- Max Verstappen: I don't need Kimi Antonelli to motivate me to stay in F1

- Valtteri Bottas to race for Cadillac in 2027 after Colton Herta 'noise'

The use of heart rate monitoring during races is not entirely new in motor racing and was debuted in F1's feeder series, Formula 2, in 2023.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said he was hopeful the Whoop partnership will add a new dimension for fans following race broadcasts.

"For the first time we'll be able to bring fans even closer to understanding what some of our drivers experience physically and mentally during the most intense moments of a race," Domenicali said. "The opportunity to uncover new insights, tell new stories and showcase the world-class athleticism that goes into making F1 one of the most extreme and exciting sports in the world, is truly groundbreaking.

"I can't wait to see these insights come to life through our broadcasts, giving fans a completely new way to experience Formula 1 while highlighting the incredible strength, resilience, and determination required to compete at the highest level of motorsport."

stories.headline: Abu Dhabi court reduces sentences for 8 in Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili brawl
stories.summary: An Abu Dhabi court has reduced the sentences of eight defendants, including six members of Team Nurmagomedov, for their part in last week's wild hotel brawl in the UAE's capital city.
stories.body:
Abu Dhabi's Criminal Court has reduced the sentences of eight defendants convicted in connection to last week's hotel brawl involving Usman Nurmagomedov and Merab Dvalishvili, according to the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department.

The eight defendants, including six members of Team Nurmagomedov, were originally sentenced to six months in prison. Under the revised ruling, which the ADJD released Tuesday, each defendant will instead pay a fine of 150,000 AED (approximately $40,800). The department said the reduced sentence followed a reconciliation between the parties, the mutual withdrawal of claims and appeal by the victim to the Abu Dhabi government for their release.

The altercation took place Nov. 11 in the lobby of the Yas Hilton Hotel, ahead of RAF's inaugural event in Abu Dhabi. Multiple videos captured Nurmagomedov, who is the PFL lightweight champion and younger cousin of Khabib Nurmagomedov, approach Dvalishvili from behind and slap him in the face, triggering a brawl between multiple members of both teams. Dvalishvili, who was initially arrested but released, advocated for Nurmagomedov's release Saturday.

Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili have been involved in a long-running feud, dating back to Dvalishvili's UFC title win against Umar Nurmagomedov, Usman's older brother, in January 2025. The camps were involved in a brief altercation at another RAF event in July in Dvalishvili's home country of Georgia. Over the weekend, UFC president Dana White criticized RAF's security measures, saying, "They must like it for this to happen all the time."

RAF founder Chad Bronstein told ESPN the organization regretted the incident, but pushed back on any suggestion it's becoming commonplace.

"Did they have drama in the past? Yeah," Bronstein said of Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili. "But did I think that was going to happen in Abu Dhabi? No. You can always expect there's going to be some words in a press conference ... I didn't think that would happen in a hotel lobby. How many fights have taken place at the UFC, at press conferences, in arenas? We have a great relationship with the UFC, but I think that's an unfair statement."

Bronstein added the incident did not impact RAF's recently-signed deal with the region of Abu Dhabi.

"We're already talking about new events coming up, we have a five-year deal," Bronstein said. "Saturday's event sold out Etihad Arena. I feel like there's going to be a long partnership."

On Monday, RAF announced Dvalishvili and his 21-year-old Georgian teammate Saba Lazishvili have been booked to the promotion's first event in the New York metropolitan area on Dec. 19 at Nassau Coliseum in Long Island.

Dvalishvili will face Kenzo Biyong, a former Dutch professional soccer player from the Netherlands. Lazashvili, who gained a massive online following for his participation in the hotel lobby brawl, will face the winner of a match between Sergio Garcia and Cody Garbrandt at RAF 15 on Nov. 28 in Chicago.

stories.headline: Nike replaces Adidas as UEFA ball provider to restyle Champions League
stories.summary: The Champions League ball will have a new look next season after Nike replaced Adidas as UEFA's official provider.
stories.body:
The Champions League ball will have a new look next season after Nike replaced Adidas as UEFA's official provider.

A match ball manufactured by Adidas, with the famous star-studded ball used for Europe's premier competition, will be used for the final time in the 2026-27 final.

There has been no confirmation as to whether the new Nike ball will retain the star pattern used in the competitions logo. UEFA said in a statement: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course.."

- Why the Champions League's iconic 'star' match ball could soon be replaced

From 2027-28, U.S. brand Nike will take over as the official ball supplier for UEFA for the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League.

German brand Adidas had been the ball supplier for the UEFA Champions League since 2001 but their long-standing association with the competition is now coming to an end.

Nike went into exclusive talks in April with the agency that handles all commercial deals for UEFA club competitions, a subsidiary of United States-based Relevent.

Relevent was appointed last year by the commercial joint venture between UEFA and the increasingly influential European Football Clubs group, which has seen long-standing sponsor deals end.

Relevent was co-founded by Miami Dolphins owner Stephen Ross and also has a long-term deal with UEFA to market commercial rights for national team competitions.

Total broadcast and sponsor revenue for UEFA men's club competitions is projected to rise above 5 billion euros ($5.5 billion) starting next season.

Camilo Andrade, Vice President and General Manager of Nike Football, said: "We are excited and honoured to return to the UEFA Champions League, one of football's biggest stages, after more than two decades, and to bring Nike match balls across UEFA's men's club competitions, including all three major competitions for the first time.

"Football is the world's game, and the ball is at the centre of it, the one thing every player, in every competition, has in common. This is a long-term commitment for Nike. We will listen to the athlete's voice, push the edges of innovation, honour the prestige and tradition of these competitions, and make sure the ball represents the instinct, creativity and joy football brings to billions of fans."

Guy-Laurent Epstein, Co-Managing Director UC3 -- which unites UEFA to Europe's clubs -- said: "We are delighted to welcome Nike as the official match ball provider for UEFA men's club competitions from 2027. Nike brings an incredible combination of sporting heritage, creativity and cultural influence, with an ability to connect with fans around the world. We look forward to working together, both on and off the pitch, to deliver innovation, quality and performance at every level of European club football."

Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.headline: First-half romp powers Jillaroos' fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup salute
stories.summary: Australia's Jillaroos have blown away New Zealand 34-10 to win a fourth-straight Women's Rugby League World Cup.
stories.body:
Australia have underlined their women's rugby league dominance with a 34-10 annihilation of New Zealand in the World Cup final.

The Jillaroos did the damage with six first-half tries on Sunday at Suncorp Stadium, with winger Jaime Chapman recording a brilliant hat-trick before the break to cap a historic tournament.

It was Australia's fourth straight Cup triumph, following a 54-4 win in the final four years ago and coming after New Zealand won the first three tournaments between 2000-08.

Chapman carried two players more than 10 metres to score her first, before flying into the corner for another and then busting through four tacklers for a sensational 70-metre solo effort.

Her treble gave her the equal record for tries in a World Cup -- for men or women -- at 13, matching the Kiwi Ferns' Honey Hireme-Smiler from 2017.

It seemed inevitable that she would go clear in the second half.

But both teams struggled in the Brisbane humidity, with the Kiwi Ferns' try in the finals seconds the only points of an error-riddled second period.

For the Jillaroos there were several poignant narratives to come out of the win.

Coach Jess Skinner's controversial decision to play five-eighth Jesse Southwell and drop Jocelyn Kelleher paid dividends.

Southwell schemed with the ball, landed five goals and was the perfect foil for half Tarryn Aiken, who controlled play with confidence and skill.

Chapman played in the pool games and semi-final in the 2022 World Cup but has now put an indelible stamp on a final.

"There is no better win than winning the World Cup on home turf," she told Channel Seven.

"We connected the first day we came into camp."

Fullback Tamika Upton sat out the tournament four years ago with a calf injury but now the five-time premiership winner has every team accolade in the game to her credit.

Prop Millie Elliott retires with a fairytale ending while dual international Sariah Paki, who was chased by the Ferns to play for them, has now won the World Cup in two sports after triumphing with the Australian rugby sevens side in 2022.

All the talk before the clash was the danger posed by New Zealand's Golden Boot winner and strike centre Stacey Waaka.

The former rugby union star, who had scored nine tries in the tournament, was snuffed out by Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly, who confronted Waaka all match and gave her no space.

As the Jillaroos' big guns stood up, centre Jessica Sergis scored her 23rd try in 18 Tests with a 70m dash through the middle off an undetected forward pass.

Aiken turned second-rower Shaylee Bent inside for the second try of the match while Upton started and finished a movement that had her attacking fingerprints all over it.

Ferns fullback Apii Nicholls was her side's best player in a dynamic display until she tore a hamstring in the 66th minute.
